query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In a non-equilibrium Mg–Al–(Cu, Zn, Gd) lightweight high-entropy alloy that has been water-quenched from the melt into a single supersaturated FCC solid solution, subsequent low-temperature aging (≈300–400 °C) triggers spinodal-like decomposition in which Mg atoms diffuse to grain boundaries and free surfaces, forming nm-scale Mg-rich hcp domains and promoting external MgO/MgAl2O4 spinel formation. 1) Internally, the Mg depletion of the FCC matrix suppresses galvanic Mg-driven anodic dissolution, lowering aqueous corrosion rates; 2) Externally, the adherent Mg-rich spinel layer reduces cation outward diffusion, cutting high-temperature (600 °C) oxidation mass-gain roughly in half relative to the as-quenched state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast Mg-rich Al-Cu-Zn-Gd high-entropy alloy (ρ ≤ 6 g cm⁻³) rapidly solidified to a single FCC supersaturated solid solution with minor retained amorphous regions; no equilibrium intermetallics or oxides present.
generation.intervention: Isothermal aging at 350 °C for 24 h in argon, producing controlled decomposition from the non-equilibrium solid solution.
generation.conditions: Subsequent tests: (a) aqueous corrosion in aerated 3.5 wt % NaCl at 25 °C, (b) cyclic oxidation at 600 °C in flowing lab air for 100 h.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of Mg-rich hcp nanoprecipitates and a continuous external MgO/MgAl2O4 spinel layer caused by selective Mg outward diffusion during aging.
generation.mechanism: Spinodal-type decomposition lowers the chemical potential of Mg by segregating it to grain boundaries and surfaces. The resulting Mg-depleted FCC matrix has a higher corrosion potential, reducing Mg-driven galvanic dissolution, while the Mg-rich surface quickly oxidises to a dense, adherent spinel that impedes further oxygen ingress.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the as-quenched baseline: (i) corrosion current density in NaCl will fall by ≈50 ± 15 %, and (ii) oxidation mass gain after 100 h at 600 °C will decrease by ≈40–60 %. TEM/EDS will reveal Mg-rich hcp domains (5–20 nm) and surface XRD will show MgAl2O4/spinel peaks absent in the baseline.
generation.baseline: As-quenched alloy measured without aging, exhibiting single-phase FCC, uniform Mg distribution, higher corrosion current, and >1 mg cm⁻² oxidation mass gain after 100 h at 600 °C.
generation.boundary: Applies to Mg-containing HEAs with 10–35 at % Mg, overall density <6 g cm⁻³, initially in a supersaturated solid-solution state; aging temperatures between 250–450 °C where diffusion of Mg is appreciable yet melting/phase-reversion is avoided. Outside this window (e.g., Mg <5 at %, aging >500 °C) the mechanism may not operate.
generation.uncertainty: Magnitude of property changes may vary with exact composition and grain size; spinodal versus classical nucleation-and-growth separation cannot be distinguished without in-situ studies.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two identical alloy batches; keep one as-quenched, age the other at 350 °C/24 h. Characterise both by TEM/EDS (precipitate presence), XRD (phase ID, oxide scale), potentiodynamic polarisation in 3.5 % NaCl, and thermogravimetric oxidation at 600 °C for 100 h.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Hypothesis is falsified if aged samples (a) do not show Mg-rich precipitates and Mg-depleted FCC matrix, OR (b) exhibit corrosion current reduction <10 % and oxidation mass-gain reduction <10 % relative to baseline, despite confirmed aging treatment.
